deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a reading excerpt in Riemann's hand, filed under the later added heading 'Raum (Materie)' (space, matter). It continues the Herbart excerpts of the previous page and runs on to the next.

(1) Bibliographic pointers to where Herbart treats space and matter, and Leibniz on them:
- Herbart, Allgemeine Metaphysik I, §115 (one word struck out), §116 ('Leibnitz u. Spalding', 'Leibnitz und Kant'; reading uncertain).
- Herbart, Lehrbuch zur Einleitung in die Philosophie, §137, noted as added in the 2nd edition of 1821.
- Herbart's Königsberg Latin dissertation 'Theoriae de attractione elementorum principia metaphysica'. Lectio I was defended on 19 June 'pro receptione' into the philosophical faculty and Lectio II on 20 June 'pro loco'. It was printed at Königsberg, typis academicis, 93 pp., 8°, 1812.
- The German companion piece 'Philosophische Aphorismen veranlasst durch eine neue Erklärung der Anziehung unter den Elementen' (Königsberger Archiv I, Heft 4, p. 545), 1812.

(2) A verbatim copy of De attr. el. §27.
- Thesis: matter cannot be defined merely as 'being in space', since the bare notion of 'Esse in spatio' is self-contradictory.
- Reason: 'Esse' expresses absolute position, while 'space' expresses a relative one. Fusing them yields a quality burdened with relations, to which absolute being cannot be referred (cross-references to §§12, 17).
- Scholion I: Leibniz saw this and therefore posited unextended monads rather than shaped atoms. Herbart quotes the opening of the theses 'written for Prince Eugene' (the Monadology §§1–3: simple substances must exist because composites exist; where there are no parts there is no extension, figure or divisibility; monads are the elements of things).
- Herbart's argument: followed consistently, 'compositum = aggregatum simplicium' gives matter made of monads alone. Leibniz, moved by the geometric notion of the continuum, instead added matter to the monads: Opera, ed. Dutens, Tom. II, p. 226, matter constituted by antitypy and extension. At p. 230 he speaks of a 'unio' or real 'unient' added by God, from which arises materia prima. At p. 294 the dilemma is that, if only monads were substances, either bodies are mere phenomena or the continuum arises from points, which is absurd. At p. 320 he says real continuity can arise only from a vinculum substantiale.
- Herbart's criticism: the vinculum is wholly relational, contains all spatial relations, oppositions and negations, and is superadded ad hoc. It has no fixed place in the system and contradicts the thesis that composites are only aggregates of simples. The sentence breaks off ('Maluit ingens vir ... in hac vitiorum congerie acquiescere') and continues on the next page.

The next page gives Riemann's own excerpt of Leibniz's letters to Des Bosses on the vinculum substantiale (Dutens II, pp. 320–322).

There is no derivation to reconstruct. The page bears on Riemann's natural-philosophical interest in Herbart's continuum and space theory, the background to his Habilitation lecture, but it contains nothing original.
errors: No mathematical steps to check. Herbart's attribution of the Monadology to 'theses written for Prince Eugene' reflects the 18th/19th-century tradition; that text was actually the 'Principes de la nature et de la grâce' or the Monadology, a common conflation. This is a slip of Herbart's, copied faithfully, not Riemann's.

results.what: Excerpt of Herbart, De attractione elementorum §27 and Scholion I: critique of Leibniz's monads and vinculum substantiale with respect to the continuum and matter in space
results.modern_name: Herbartian critique of the Leibnizian continuum / monadology (philosophy of space and matter)
results.usually_credited_to: J. F. Herbart (1812); Leibniz (Monadology 1714; Des Bosses correspondence 1706–1716)

results.what: Bibliographic notes locating Herbart's discussions of space/matter (Metaphysik §§115–116, Einleitung §137, 2nd ed. 1821)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a straight copy of Herbart's Latin text plus references. Riemann's close study of Herbart is well documented, including his own statement that he was a Herbartian in psychology and epistemology. There is no mathematics and nothing original.
transcription_corrections: Line 1: the word after '§.115.' is struck out and illegible. The reading 'Leibnitz u. Spalding' is uncertain from the image.
The image consistently has 'Leibnitius'. The transcription's 'Leibnitzius' in Scholion I should read 'Leibnitius'.
The marginal 'p. 230' is written above 'extensionem. Alio autem loco'. It is a page reference to Dutens II, not part of the Latin text. Likewise 'pag 294' is written above 'addat'.
'id quod saepius[?] injecerat': the image suggests a different adverb, possibly 'saepiuscule'. It remains uncertain and is not simply a repeat of the preceding 'Saepius'.
'nudam quam materiam' is the reading of the image, though 'nudam qua materiam' is also possible.
